key_concept: Oxygen ($2p^4$) has a lower first ionization enthalpy than nitrogen because removing one electron leaves the stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration and relieves pairing repulsion. Fluorine is higher than oxygen simply because its nuclear charge is larger.
steps: Write the valence configurations: N $= 2s^2 2p^3$ (half-filled), O $= 2s^2 2p^4$ (one $2p$ orbital doubly occupied), F $= 2s^2 2p^5$.

Recall the approximate values of $\Delta_i H_1$: N $\approx 1402$, O $\approx 1314$, F $\approx 1681\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. So $\Delta_i H_1(\text{O}) < \Delta_i H_1(\text{N})$ and $\Delta_i H_1(\text{O}) < \Delta_i H_1(\text{F})$, and Assertion A is correct.

Ionizing O gives $\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}^+ + e^-$, with $\text{O}^+ = 2s^2 2p^3$. This is an exactly half-filled $p$ subshell, which is extra stable because of symmetry and exchange energy. Reason R is correct.

Losing an electron from O is easier because the electron removed is the paired one, which feels interelectronic repulsion. Its removal produces the stable $2p^3$ arrangement, so less energy is needed. This is why O falls below N, which breaks the general left-to-right increase.
Oxygen is also below fluorine because F has a higher nuclear charge across the period. The NTA key treats R as the correct explanation of the anomalous dip at O.
The key's verdict is that both A and R are correct and R explains A, which matches Option (1).
final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
why_not_others: Option (2) fails because the half-filled $\text{O}^+$ ($2p^3$) configuration is the accepted reason for the dip in ionization enthalpy at O. Options (3) and (4) fail because both A and R are factually true.
common_trap: Students often assume ionization enthalpy rises steadily from N to O to F and mark A false, forgetting the N > O anomaly caused by the half-filled $2p^3$ stability of N and $\text{O}^+$.
time_saving_tip: Memorise the second-period anomalies directly: Be > B and N > O. The cause is always a stable filled or half-filled subshell, either in the parent atom or in the ion formed.
